newsitem.title: GERMANY: Top institute says Germany needs Maastricht leeway.
newsitem.headline: Top institute says Germany needs Maastricht leeway.

text.p: Leading German research institute DIW said on Saturday Germany had no chance of hitting the budget deficit level required to launch the euro in 1999 and should exploit the leeway offered by the Maastricht Treaty.

In an interview with the daily Neue Osnabruecker Zeitung, DIW budget expert Dieter Vesper predicted that Germany's 1997 budget deficit would reach 3.5 percent of GDP, well beyond the three percent threshold required for EMU.
But Vesper noted that there was room for manoeuvre on the numerical thresholds set out in the Maastricht Treaty.
"Chancellor (Helmut) Kohl and (Finance Minister Theo) Waigel should therefore not be more pope-like than the Pope, and use that leeway," he said.

So far Germany has insisted it can still get its deficit in line to make the EMU grade this year, despite concern over its record unemployment levels which are eating into tax returns and inflating social security spending.

To qualify for Europe's Economic and Monetary Union (EMU), contenders are expected to keep their national budget deficits for 1997 below three percent of GDP and debt below 60 percent of GDP, with a small amount of leeway expected.
Vesper said Germany would fail to get its deficit in hand this year even if it introduced more social welfare cutbacks or tax increases.

German tax returns would be six or seven billion marks lower than the latest government estimates. Meanwhile debt levels were rising, making a nonsense of Bonn's confidence that it will keep the German deficit below three percent of GDP.
